ARKI: Exposure to an actively managed innovation fund wrapped in a buffer structure for a twelve-month outcome period starting in the second quarter, softening part of any loss while capping gains. It layers defense on an already volatile growth fund, so the cushion matters more than the cap.
ASD: Companies supporting the autism community worldwide: therapy and education providers, diagnostic and treatment developers, and researchers serving neurodivergent people. It is an impact-themed health care bet: most of the fund is health care stocks, chosen for their role in one cause rather than broad returns.
BABW: Leveraged exposure to Alibaba through swaps on its shares, structured to pay distributions every week. It is a short-term trading tool on one Chinese tech giant: leverage magnifies Alibaba's moves, and weekly payouts come from the swap structure, not from dividends.
BIOY: Weekly income from selling put options on a leveraged biotechnology fund that triples its index's daily moves. It stacks an income strategy on the market's most headline-driven sector: biotech already swings on trial results, and triple leverage multiplies every jump and drop.
CGPT: Companies that run AI inference, the behind-the-scenes computing that answers prompts and powers AI features in real time, all in the technology sector. It is a focused bet on the usage phase of AI rather than the training phase, riding data-center demand.
CJUL: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in July, with gains capped in exchange. The July start fixes the terms: this edition's protection clock runs from mid-year, and later buyers get what remains.
CJUN: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in June, with gains capped in exchange. The mid-year start fixes its terms, so buyers later inherit only the protection time that remains.
CLIM: Real estate investment trusts around the world screened for climate resilience: property owners judged better prepared for floods, heat and other weather risks. It is a property income holding with an environmental filter, so the usual REIT risks come with a climate scorecard attached.
DIPR: Companies building space systems and satellite communications: the networks that provide connectivity, navigation, sensing and data from orbit. It is an actively managed growth bet on the orbital economy, mixing industrials with technology and even some private holdings, so valuations can be murkier than usual.
DRVR: S&P 500 companies chosen for the dividends they pay and the payout growth behind them, spread across financials, consumer and technology stocks. It is a large-cap income holding with a quality tilt: the screen favors firms whose dividends look sustainable, not just the highest yielders.
DVQQ: Nasdaq-100 exposure that dials itself up or down to hold annual volatility near a 22% target, adding cash when markets get wild. It is a risk-managed growth holding: the automatic throttle smooths the ride somewhat, but it can be underinvested right when rallies start.
DVSP: S&P 500 exposure that dials itself up or down to hold annual volatility near a 20% target, parking the rest in cash when markets swing. It is a risk-managed core holding: the throttle trades some upside for a steadier path, and can lag when markets snap back.
EHCC: Exposure to ether, the Ethereum network's token, through ether funds, combined with sold call options that generate income and cap the gains. It is an income twist on crypto: premiums pay regularly, but the fund still falls with ether and misses the biggest rallies.
EYES: Companies in data and surveillance technology: the firms that collect, secure and analyze information for monitoring, security and compliance. It is a focused technology bet on the watching economy, a theme with real demand and real controversy, which can bring regulatory swings.
FCFY: S&P 500 companies with the highest free cash flow yield in each sector, so every industry is represented by its strongest cash generators. It is a value-leaning quality holding: the sector-by-sector design keeps it diversified, while the cash-flow screen favors profitable firms over story stocks.
GLAM: Companies in beauty, skincare and aesthetics: cosmetics brands, skincare makers and the retailers and clinics that sell them, mostly consumer staples and health care. It is an actively managed theme bet on the beauty business, riding consumer trends that can shift with fashion and social media.
GLCR: Icelandic companies: the banks, seafood and food firms, health care names and property companies of one small island economy. It is a single-country bet on a tiny market: a handful of stocks carry the fund, and the Icelandic krona adds currency swings on top.
GXPE: US energy companies weighted by their full market value, with no size adjustments: oil and gas producers, pipelines and refiners at their natural weights. It is a pure sector bet, which means the giant integrated oil companies dominate and the fund swings with energy prices.
HJLY: S&P 500 exposure through options built to protect against all losses over an outcome period that started in July, with gains capped in exchange for that full protection. It is the defensive extreme of its series: principal protection for the period, paid for with a tight cap.
IDAU: Developed-market stocks outside North America, in Europe, Japan and similar economies, wrapped in options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in August. It pairs foreign diversification with late-summer protection terms: gains are capped, and currency swings still show through.
IDJL: Developed-market stocks outside North America, in Europe, Japan and similar economies, wrapped in options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in July. It pairs foreign exposure with mid-year defense: gains are capped, and currency moves still play a part.
IDMY: Developed-market stocks outside the United States, in Europe, Japan and similar economies, wrapped in options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in May. It pairs foreign diversification with defense: gains are capped, and currency moves still matter.
IDVY: Dividend-paying companies outside the United States with records of growing their payouts, led by financials and industrials in developed markets. It is a foreign income holding: the rising-dividend screen favors established payers, and currency swings add a second source of movement.
ISRL: The 120 largest companies in Israel by market value, led by financials with real estate, technology and industrials behind them. It is a single-country bet on a small, export-driven market: currency swings, regional politics and a handful of giant firms drive most of the result.
JQTY: US companies screened for quality: businesses with strong balance sheets and consistent profitability, led by technology at a bit over a third. It is a core holding with a sturdiness filter: the screen favors firms built to weather downturns, so it can lag speculative rallies.
JUNC: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in June, with gains capped in exchange. The June start fixes the terms: the shallower buffer suits investors who accept smaller drops in exchange for a higher cap.
MRA: An autocallable note tied to a single stock, MARA, the bitcoin mining company, a structured contract that pays income and can end early if the stock behaves. It is concentrated income with heavy fine print: the underlying miner already swings wildly with bitcoin prices.
MTYY: Weekly income from selling options on a leveraged fund tied to Strategy, the software firm turned bitcoin holding company. It stacks options on leverage on a stock that already amplifies bitcoin, so the swings are extreme in both directions and holding periods should be short.
MUY: Options on a single stock, Micron, the memory chipmaker, arranged to pay income while following its share price up to a limit on gains. It is a concentrated income bet on one cyclical chip stock: payouts come from its swings, and memory downturns hit it hard.
NYYY: Daily income built around NVIDIA, using Treasury bills and short-term funds as ballast while options on the chip giant generate payouts. It is an income machine bolted onto one volatile stock: the bills keep most of the money steady, but the payouts rise and fall with NVIDIA's swings.
QAU: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in August. It is tech growth with late-summer protection terms: the shallower buffer leaves a higher cap on gains.
QJL: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in July. It is tech growth with a mid-year safety net: the shallower buffer leaves more room to gain than deeper versions.
QQAU: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in August. It blends tech growth with late-summer defense: gains are capped, and the August start fixes the protection terms.
QQJL: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in July. It blends tech growth with mid-year protection terms: gains are capped, and the July start fixes what protection remains.
QQJN: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in June. It is tech exposure with mid-year protection terms: the cap limits rallies, and the June start fixes the buffer.
QSE: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in September. It is tech growth with autumn protection terms: gains are capped, and the September start date fixes the buffer.
ROBX: The ten standout companies in robotics, from factory automation to surgical and warehouse robots, mostly industrials with a technology slice. It is a concentrated bet on machines doing physical work: ten names carry the fund, so it swings with automation headlines and orders.
SCAU: Small US companies through options on a small-cap fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in August. It adds late-summer defense to the market's jumpiest tier: the buffer helps, but small-cap swings and the gain cap both bind.
SEPC: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in September, with gains capped in exchange. The autumn start fixes its terms: later buyers get the remaining protection, not a fresh period.
TECY: Weekly income from selling put options on a leveraged technology fund that triples its index's daily moves. It is an aggressive income trade on the tech sector: the triple leverage underneath makes payouts and losses both extreme, so it is built for short holding periods.
TGRZ: Chinese companies building large language models and AI foundation technology: the firms racing to match Western AI with their own models and cloud platforms. It is a single-country bet on the most contested corner of tech, so export controls and Chinese policy hit it directly.
TKNQ: Companies building tokenization technology: the platforms turning real-world assets like property and bonds into tradeable digital tokens, mostly financial firms. It is a focused bet on finance moving on-chain, mixing payment and exchange stocks with crypto funds, so sentiment swings it hard.
TNUK: Companies across the nuclear energy chain: uranium and fuel, plant builders and operators, and utilities running reactors, split among industrials, utilities and energy. It is a focused bet on a nuclear revival driven by AI power demand, swinging with uranium prices and politics.
TXBC: The ten largest crypto assets excluding bitcoin: ether and the other big networks, reached through regulated instruments rather than direct coin holdings. It is the crypto market without its anchor: removing bitcoin makes it more volatile, since smaller coins swing harder in both directions.
VEGX: Large companies outside the United States screened to exclude animal exploitation: no meat, dairy, animal testing or other animal-derived businesses. It is a values-based foreign holding led by technology and industrials: the vegan screen removes whole industries, so it will not mirror a plain international fund.
VPFF: US preferred shares and hybrid securities, mostly from banks, utilities and health care issuers, which pay fixed dividends like bonds but sit lower in line than debt. It is an actively managed income holding: payouts run higher than bonds, with more price risk if issuers wobble.
WSPC: Companies in the space economy worldwide: launch providers, satellite operators and the firms supplying them, mostly industrials. It is an actively managed growth bet on orbit as a business, where the manager picks winners in an industry still short on profits and long on ambition.
XVAZ: Amazon shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding: Amazon's retail and cloud fortunes drive everything, and the options swap some of that upside for regular payouts.
XVGL: Alphabet shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding on Google's parent: the options harvest its steady climb for payouts, trading away some upside.
XVMT: Meta Platforms shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding on the social media giant: payouts are the plan, but Meta's swings still drive the outcome.
